1.pericope_label: Now the Lord had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father’s house, unto a land that I will shew thee: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing: And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.

schools.summary: Settle the tense against the tradition, since the Hebrew reads simply and Jehovah said and the rendering had said was adopted only to accommodate Stephen's speech, while it is the manner of the narrative to revert to its own starting point; take the phrase thy country as proof that Abram and his father were no new settlers at Ur but a family long established there; and state the shape of the word itself, that it carried a command and a promise together, and that what Abram was to leave was everything — country, kindred and father's house.

Rule out the ordinary motives for emigration one by one — not levity as with rash and fickle men, not disgust with one's own country as with morose persons, not flight from crime, not any foolish hope — since Abram did not move a foot but as he was guided; argue that the call came once and in Chaldea, because a command to depart from one's land and father's house would be superfluous to a man already sojourning as a stranger; and explain why a promise is annexed to the command at all, since we are slothful to obey and faith cannot stand except on the promises while obedience is produced by faith alone.

Report the dissension over one call or two and come down for two on the authority of Hales, the first omitted from the Old Testament but recorded in the speech of Stephen and the second recorded only here, with the tense as part of the evidence; hear in the promise of a great name the coming change from a high father to the father of a multitude; and read the promise of a nation as relief and trial at once, relief because Abram had no child and trial because his wife had long been barren, so that belief must be against hope, resting on the power that raises up children out of stones.

Find the design of the call double, to try Abram's faith and obedience and to separate him and set him apart for God and for services and favours yet to come; and take the circumstances from Stephen's speech, where the God of glory appeared to him in such displays of glory as left no room to doubt the divine authority of what was said.

debates.question: Was Abram called once or twice?

sides.position: Twice: the first call omitted in the Old Testament but recorded in Stephen's speech, the second recorded only here, as the tense the Lord said rather than had said shows
Twice, in two appearances, the same words or very near the same being spoken at Ur and again at Haran after Terah's death
Once, in Chaldea: a command to leave one's land and father's house would be superfluous to a man already sojourning elsewhere, and Stephen testifies the appearance came before Charran
The Hebrew reads simply and Jehovah said; had said was adopted to accommodate Stephen, but the narrative is merely reverting to its starting point

outliers.note: Alone rules out four ordinary motives for emigration in a row — levity, disgust with one’s country, flight from crime, and foolish hope — in order to leave divine command as the only account of the departure.
Alone reports the state of the question about one call or two as a standing dissension among commentators, and adopts Hales’s reconstruction with the tense of the verb as part of the evidence.

themes: get thee out of thy country
I will make of thee a great nation

4.pericope_label: So Abram departed, as the Lord had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran. And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.

schools.summary: Supply the likelier reason for the long halt, that Abram stayed at Haran only on his father's account and resumed the journey at his death; read the substance as wealth of every kind rather than cattle only, and infer from a man very rich in silver and gold that he had engaged in trade during those years and so may have known the caravan routes; and settle the disputed phrase by ruling that these are not souls whom they had begotten but the male and female slaves that Abram and Lot had acquired.

Close the earlier argument on this verse, since those who place the call at Charran lay hold of these words, and answer that Moses is simply returning to the thread of his history after giving the cause of the departure; then stop on the phrase about souls to remark that this is the first mention of servitude in the Scriptures, and reason from it that not long after the deluge the wickedness of man made liberty, common by nature to all, perish for a great part of mankind — whether by the laws of war, whence the very name of bondman comes, or by want, the order of nature was violently infringed.

Take the souls for proselytes whom Abram had persuaded to worship the true God, borrowing a rabbi's phrase about souls gathered under the wings of the divine Majesty, while allowing elsewhere that the words may equally cover persons employed in his service; and work the chronology from the two ages given, so that Terah was a hundred and thirty at Abram's birth and the seventieth year named earlier belongs to Haran instead.

Make the obedience the substance of the verse, speedy and without delay, submissive and without dispute, since he went out not knowing whither he went but knowing whom he followed; and take the age as an aggravation of the same virtue, seventy-five being a time for rest and settlement, so that here is an instance of an old convert beginning the world again.

debates.question: Who were the souls they had gotten in Haran?

sides.position: Proselytes whom Abram had persuaded to worship the true God and to go with him
holders: the Chaldee paraphrasts (as reported by Clarke)

sides.position: Either those employed in his service or those he had converted; the phrase will bear both
Chiefly dependents and slaves, though converts may also have been in the company
Male and female servants, not souls whom they had begotten

outliers.note: Alone turns the phrase about souls into an excursus on the origin of servitude, dating the loss of natural liberty to shortly after the deluge and tracing the name of bondman to capture in war, while holding that the order of nature was violently infringed however it began.
Alone infers commercial activity from the wealth, supposing that Abram traded during the years at Haran and may thereby have learned the routes the caravans took.

themes: into the land of Canaan they came

6.pericope_label: And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land. And the Lord appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the Lord, who appeared unto him. And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Beth–el, and pitched his tent, having Beth–el on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the Lord, and called upon the name of the Lord. And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.

schools.summary: Begin from the ground, since Shechem means shoulder and named the ridge joining Ebal and Gerizim, a name drawn from the conformation of the land and so possibly very ancient; treat the removals as needing no special explanation, breaking camp being the ordinary condition of nomad life and wealth in cattle forcing frequent changes; fix the encampment with Ai to the east and Bethel to the west, noting that the later name is used ahead of its time since the place was still called Luz; and mark the appearance as a first of its kind, all previous communication having been direct and without visible medium.

Count the removals and deny that Abram ran hither and thither for his own gratification like light-minded persons, since necessities drove him out to teach him by continual habit that he was not merely a stranger but a wanderer in the land of which he was lord — and turn the reproof on the reader, that if he bore his wanderings patiently our fastidiousness is inexcusable when we murmur at being denied a quiet nest; then observe what the divine help actually consisted of, a bare word offered to a childless old man with a barren wife, insipid consolation to the flesh though faith has a different taste.

Measure how little comfort the arrival brought, since one would have expected the kings of Canaan to surrender their crowns and instead he comes without observation and little notice is taken of him, God still willing that he should live by faith and look on Canaan as a land of promise even while standing in it — not having it to himself, and unlikely to get ground to pitch his tent on except by the permission of its inhabitants.

Correct the rendering of the tree, since the word is oak and not plain, the Septuagint giving the lofty oak and the place likely known for a grove of them; refuse the usual inference from the notice that the Canaanite was then in the land, which is thought an interpolation on the ground that it must postdate the conquest, when it states only what was true at the time; and turn the altar into a rule for householders, that where a man has a tent God must have an altar, since a house in which the worship of God is not established cannot be reckoned under divine protection.

debates.question: Is the notice that the Canaanite was then in the land a later insertion?

sides.position: It is thought an interpolation, since the words must postdate the expulsion under Joshua — but this by no means follows, as Moses states only what was true when Abram passed through
It states the plain difficulty of Abram's position, that he had not the land to himself and could not pitch his tent except by the inhabitants' permission

debates.question: Should the tree at Moreh be called a plain or an oak?

sides.position: An oak, the Septuagint giving the lofty oak, the place being likely known for a grove or for one tree of stupendous bulk
A terebinth rather than an oak, the two words being interchanged in many manuscripts because the trees resemble each other in foliage and bark
The oak of Moreh, the same tree under which Jacob afterwards buried the strange gods

outliers.note: Alone turns the altar into a rule for householders, asking how few who build houses ever think of the necessity of building an altar, and holding that a house without the worship of God cannot be reckoned under divine protection.
Alone brings a modern traveller’s description of the valley of Shechem as an oasis of remarkable beauty set like Damascus in a desert and girt with barren mountains.

themes: the Canaanite was then in the land

10.pericope_label: And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land. And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife, Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon: Therefore it shall come to pass, when the Egyptians shall see thee, that they shall say, This is his wife: and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive. Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.

schools.summary: Explain the famine physically, since rain falls in Palestine at only two seasons so that the failure of either is felt at once in a dry region with no means of bringing food from a distance, while Egypt, watered by the Nile's flooding from Abyssinian rains, probably had not suffered; use the same event to date the episode, since only about eight years are left between the arrival in Canaan and the birth of Ishmael; and state the objection to Abram's words in its exact form, that they were true literally, Sarai being Terah's daughter, and absolutely false, since they implied she was wholly his sister and therefore not his wife.

Recall the abundance Abram had been used to in Chaldea and at Charran, so that being driven out by hunger from the very land where he had promised himself a happy life was a temptation to the quick; then treat what he did next as a rock on which many strike, weighing it in both directions: there is something of falsehood in the dissimulation, and though he afterwards pleads that he feigned nothing untrue, he was greatly culpable in stripping his wife's chastity of its legitimate defence, so that it was no doing of his that she was not prostituted.

Note that this is the first famine on record and that it fell on the most fertile land then under the sun; call the words about the sister a suppressing of part of the truth rather than the telling of an untruth, and supply the relationship from the later chapter as a sister by the same father and a different mother, while reporting and rejecting the conjecture that she was rather Haran's daughter; then ask what will become of the willows when the cedars are so shaken.

Set out the two things the famine tried at once, what Abram would think of the God who brought him there, since nothing short of a strong faith could keep up good thoughts of him under such a providence, and what he would think of the land of promise, whether the grant of it were worth accepting as a consideration for the country he had relinquished.

debates.question: How far is Abram to be blamed for the words about his sister?

sides.position: Greatly culpable, since by concealing the marriage he stripped his wife's chastity of its legitimate defence, whatever he afterwards pleaded about not feigning an untruth

Criminal, though not a direct lie, since it concealed the truth, endangered her, and showed distrust of divine protection — proof that the strongest believer may fall in the very grace for which he is most eminent
Not a falsehood but the suppressing of part of the truth, she being his sister by the same father
True literally and absolutely false, since it implied she was wholly his sister and therefore not his wife

outliers.note: Alone uses the famine to date the episode, reckoning from Abram’s age at Haran and Ishmael’s at his father’s ninety-ninth year that only about eight years are available for everything recorded between.
Alone pairs the two trials as complementary lessons, the famine teaching Abram that even in the promised land food comes from the Lord, and Egypt teaching him that earthly craft is soon put to shame.

14.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair. The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house. And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels. And the Lord plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram’s wife. And Pharaoh called Abram, and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife? Why saidst thou, She is my sister? so I might have taken her to me to wife: now therefore behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way. And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.

schools.summary: Find the wording of the plague verse decisive, since had Moses said only that the king was punished for adultery it would not appear that Sarai's chastity was cared for, whereas he says plainly that the house was plagued because of Abram's wife, so that God interposed his mighty hand in time; notice that no answer from Abram is recorded and allow that he may simply have assented to a just reproof, while observing that he relapsed into the same fault later; and read the safe-conduct as protection rather than expulsion, since a man suddenly grown rich would seem to be carrying spoil away.

Pursue the royal title, taking Pharaoh for the common appellation of the shepherd kings who had conquered the land, a word supposed to mean king in the old Egyptian though the Hebrew root would yield the sense of being free, which such freebooters might naturally assume; use the list of gifts to fix the vocabulary of the Pentateuch, where the word for sheep comes from a root meaning to be plentiful and covers goats as well; admit that the plagues are unknown while inferring from Pharaoh's response that some knowledge of the true religion survived in Egypt; and draw from the rebuke that good people too often suspect others beyond what there is cause for.

Set the episode in its Egyptian history, where Canaan was the highway into Egypt and Semitic immigration heavy enough to overspread the Delta and at length seize the throne, so that a sheik of Abram's weight arriving at the frontier wall would be questioned by the scribes and reported to the king; read the presents as evidence of good faith, since it was usual to pay a woman's relatives on taking her to wife; defend the mention of asses against a charge of anachronism from the tombs of Benihassan; and suggest that a months-long probation before marriage was what actually saved Sarai.

Read the court with contempt, calling the princes who commended Sarai to their master pimps rather, and noting that they praised her not for what was really her praise — her virtue and modesty, her faith and piety, which were no excellencies in their eyes — but only for the beauty they judged too good for the embraces of a subject, so that she was taken into the royal house as Esther was into the seraglio.

debates.question: What were the plagues on Pharaoh's house?

sides.position: Unknown, though from the parallel case possibly barrenness in the women of the household; the phrase seems to imply more
Perhaps the ulcers the Jews speak of, and falling on the courtiers who were accessory as well as on the king
Whatever they were, the point is that Moses says the house was plagued because of Abram's wife, which shows God interposed to prevent the violation
Troubles marked enough to alarm Pharaoh during the interval before the marriage, so that Sarai was probably saved by the customary probation

outliers.note: Alone reconstructs the frontier procedure, with the wall and chain of fortresses built to keep out Semitic immigration and the Egyptian scribes interrogating so powerful a sheik and reporting him to the king.

Alone uses the list of Pharaoh’s gifts as an occasion to fix the vocabulary of the Pentateuch, deriving the word for sheep from a root meaning to be plentiful and noting that it covers goats as the Latin term covers small cattle.
